summary.headline: Narayana Q4 FY26: India margin rose to 25.1% (from 21.5%), but consolidated EBITDA dipped to ~20% on UK acquisition costs; management gives no formal guidance.
summary.overview: Management highlighted high-end case mix and robotic cardiac volumes (about 100 robotic cardiac cases a month in Bangalore) driving India ARPP and margin gains. The UK business (PPG, acquired with five months in FY26) diluted consolidated margins and PAT; management says ~200 bps of the ~500 bps margin drop was one-time deal costs, normalising to ~22%. Cayman insurance losses (USD 5 million in the quarter) remain high, with a loss ratio of about 110–112% and price increases from June. India clinics continue to lose cash because of corporate overheads, and FY26 greenfield capex was only INR 109 crore against INR 424 crore planned.

segments.name: India hospitals
segments.commentary: Margin 25.1% vs 21.5% a year ago, attributed to transformation initiatives, robotic cardiac and high-end transplant work, and higher-configuration beds; volumes stagnated while ARPP grew. Mumbai (SRCC) broke even in Q4.

segments.name: India clinics and insurance
segments.commentary: Clinic and insurance losses flat at ~INR 66 crore in FY26; management expects similar cash burn into FY27 as 11 Bangalore clinics expand and Kolkata is added, and clinics will be merged into hospital reporting from FY27.

segments.name: UK (PPG)
segments.commentary: Five months consolidated in FY26; acquisition costs and transition/IT separation costs weighed on margin, and PAT is negative mainly from amortisation. Management says cash PAT covers the GBP 150 million 7-year loan, which is serviced in the UK.

segments.name: Cayman Islands (insurance and hospital)
segments.commentary: Insurance loss ratio around 110–112% (CIMA data); price increases on 30–35% of accounts in June; hospital revenue growth expected to slow from double digits as new client additions are slowed. Management asks analysts to view insurance and hospital together.

guidance_outlook: No formal guidance; management declined to give ARPOB or top-line targets, saying rack-rate and price increases run at low-to-mid single digits.
Insurance losses expected to decline over about three quarters after June price increases; one or two more quarters of losses in the current range are possible.
Overheads expected to fall after UK integration; no date given for India insurance breakeven.
India capex of INR 3,000 crore across projects, with about INR 1,000 crore each expected to commission in FY28 and FY29; FY28 Rajarhat, HSR, Raipur and Bangalore timelines reaffirmed.
No additional capex planned for Cayman; UK capex plan to be shared later.
Mumbai expected to turn around once the adult programme starts; Bangalore clinics and Kolkata clinics planned in FY27.
capex_capacity: FY26 greenfield capex INR 109 crore against INR 424 crore planned; management blamed election-related labour shortages and permission delays.
Raipur: new tower to replace an old building; full capability set in place, no hospital-specific data shared.
Kolkata (RN Tagore) campus about 3.5 acres; Rajarhat project to add integrated quaternary capacity. Kolkata bone marrow transplant beds 10 versus 45 in Bangalore.
Management says construction costs are up about 60% over five years, and new hospitals are being built with more automation.
Clinic plan to double the current clinic count, with pace tied to property acquisition, rent negotiation and fit-outs.
demand_pricing: Bangalore: about 100 robotic cardiac cases a month and about 160 percutaneous aortic valve procedures in the cath lab; highest paediatric bone marrow transplant volumes.
North (NCR): management concedes it is very competitive; the cluster grew 7.5% in FY26 and Gurgaon/Dharamshila strategy is unchanged with no expansion plans.
Kolkata revenue share 26% growing only 5–6%; management expects volume growth in the next 2–3 quarters from digital marketing and clinics.
Patient volumes stagnated in FY26 while ARPP grew, as the mix shifted to advanced procedures and payer mix changed.
UK private-pay share was 7% at acquisition; management reports an absolute increase but gave no current figure.
Overheads rose ~8% against 10.2% revenue growth due to power and minimum wage inflation plus one-time merger costs.

qa_highlights.question: Why are Cayman insurance losses so high, and when do they reach breakeven?
qa_highlights.answer: Anesh Shetty said premium ramped faster than expected to ~USD 60 million annualised; losses should drop over about three quarters after June price increases and account pruning. Loss ratio is ~110–112% per CIMA data.

qa_highlights.question: Is UK EBITDA margin improvement sustainable and where did cost cuts come from?
qa_highlights.answer: Sandhya J said only two months of data existed at acquisition, and most savings are in overheads; IT separation is ongoing and a few more quarters are needed. Management expects overs and unders to neutralise.

qa_highlights.question: Why did India margins expand and is 25% stable?
qa_highlights.answer: Venkatesh cited transformation initiatives, high-end procedures, robotic cardiac volumes and higher-configuration beds; he said gains are sustainable but cited crude and dollar headwinds.

qa_highlights.question: Will the UK loan be serviced given weak PAT?
qa_highlights.answer: Sandhya J said the GBP 150 million loan is serviced in the UK, the acquisition debt sits on the target's books, and cash PAT covers debt service; PAT is hit by amortisation of non-cash expenses.

qa_highlights.question: What is the Cayman hospital growth outlook?
qa_highlights.answer: Anesh Shetty said double-digit quarterly top-line growth is not sustainable and new client additions are being slowed, while hospital margins were preserved.

qa_highlights.question: Why was FY26 greenfield capex well below plan?
qa_highlights.answer: Viren Shetty said election-related labour shortages and permission delays caused the miss; FY28 commissioning goals remain.

risks_watch: Cayman insurance loss ratio ~110–112% and whether losses fall after June 2026 price increases and account purges.
UK margin and cost normalisation after IT separation; reclassification between UK and ex-UK lines makes quarter comparisons hard.
India clinic cash burn rising with 11 Bangalore clinics expanding and Kolkata clinics in FY27.
Greenfield capex execution (INR 3,000 crore program, FY28–29 commissioning) after the FY26 miss.
Overhead inflation (power, minimum wages) and volume stagnation in India.
ROCE and ROE dilution during the expansion phase, per management.
summary.management_tone: Confident on India margins and high-end procedure growth, but defensive on UK and Cayman numbers, repeatedly asking analysts to wait for more quarters and to view Cayman insurance and hospital together. Declined forward guidance on margins, ARPOB, top line and insurance breakeven; some reclassification questions were deferred to offline IR calls.
key_quotes: So we run pharmacies in all our hospitals and in all our clinics.
The FY '28 goal still remains the case, and a lot of this work can pick up now that things have normalized.
We do not believe that either ARPOB or occupancy is a correct measure of performance.
